source.title: RAIGen: Rare Attribute Identification in Text-to-Image Generative Models
source.authors: S. V. Sreelatha; Dan Wang; S. Belongie; Muhammad Awais; Anjan Dutta

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies interpretability of sparse-autoencoder features in text-to-image diffusion models, but does not test whether ordinary network neurons respond to unrelated inputs or measure polysemanticity as defined in any claim version.
record.gate_note: The closest results concern coherence and fragmentation of discovered sparse features. They do not measure the incidence of neurons responding to unrelated inputs, or test whether such mixtures share a feature used by the model. Related findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper uses sparse-autoencoder features (called 'neurons') as a tool for rare-attribute discovery in diffusion models and reports its own method's performance. It never measures whether the diffusion model's own neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Its 'neurons' are SAE latents, not network neurons. It relies on the premise that raw representations are entangled and need decomposing, so T4 fits better than T6.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that RAIGen, combining Matryoshka SAEs with a minority score, discovers encoded but underexpressed attributes across Stable Diffusion variants, SDXL and FLUX, supporting auditing and prompt-based amplification. They acknowledge in the limitations that results depend on the SAE and that some features are noisy.
record.recipe_differences: RAIGen is a rare-attribute discovery framework for diffusion models, not a reproduction or test of the original neuron-polysemanticity methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that feature interpretability depends on the decomposition method and sparsity configuration; they also describe weaker interpretability at the selected FLUX hook point than for U-Net bottlenecks.

fits_no_version.finding: A vanilla SAE fragmented concepts across latents (e.g., separate right-eye and left-eye latents); the MSAE coarse level reduced this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE decomposition choice affects whether diffusion-model concepts appear as coherent or fragmented features.

fits_no_version.finding: Low minority-score MSAE latents were diffuse; dominant attributes appeared spread across many correlated latents.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dominant (high-variance) attributes in diffusion representations are distributed across multiple SAE latents, while rare attributes form single coherent latents.

fits_no_version.finding: FLUX.1-schnell had more high-scoring but weakly interpretable features than U-Net models, attributed to architecture and hook point.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature interpretability in diffusion models varies with architecture and hook point.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The closest neuron-coherence findings are qualitative and specific to sparse-autoencoder features in diffusion models; they do not evaluate the claim's polysemanticity construct. The paper also notes that some features are noisy or ambiguous and that results depend on the autoencoder's captured features and training dynamics.
record.rows_left_out: No further results were included because the remaining reported metrics concern rare-attribute discovery, attribute presence, or prompt-based amplification rather than neuron polysemanticity.

untested.parts: No measurement of image-classifier neurons responding to unrelated inputs.
No language-model MLP neurons are studied.
No test of superposition as the cause of polysemanticity.
No test of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
No polysemantic-neuron share is measured across architectures or activation functions.
No reanalysis of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No test of how activation range or scoring changes polysemanticity judgments.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation 'discusses' is changed to 'uses_without_test'/T4, because the paper uses SAE decomposition as an instrument and evaluates only its own pipeline. Throughout the paper, 'neuron' means an SAE latent, not a model neuron. No version is tested.

versions.untested_parts: Whether neurons in image classifiers such as InceptionV1 respond to unrelated input kinds.
Transformer language models and the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or by representing more features than neurons.
Whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
The share of polysemantic neurons across activation functions, architectures, or regularization settings, and any performance cost of reducing that share.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons actually detect a shared feature or related jobs rather than unrelated mixtures.
Whether polysemanticity judgments change with activation range examined or explanation-scoring method.

rows.subject: SD v1.4
rows.operation_detail: Visualized top-activating samples and heatmaps for minority features found with a vanilla SAE.
rows.measure: Qualitative feature coherence and fragmentation across neurons
rows.baseline: MSAE comparison described in the text
rows.value: SAE neurons captured meaningful localized features, but concepts were often fragmented across neurons; one example split the right and left eye across two neurons.
rows.note: The reported fragmentation is across neurons, not a measurement of one neuron responding to unrelated inputs.
rows.check: Concerns fragmentation of SAE latents (left/right eye split), not polysemanticity of network neurons. The vanilla SAE vs MSAE contrast compares the study's own method variants, so this is arguably not a claim-relevant row.

rows.subject: SD v1.4
rows.operation_detail: Visualized low-scoring coarse-level MSAE neurons and their activation heatmaps.
rows.measure: Qualitative semantic coherence of neuron activations
rows.baseline: Higher-ranked minority neurons, described as sharp and semantically coherent
rows.value: Bottom-ranked neurons were described as diffuse, fragmented, and unreliable for interpreting dominant features; dominant features appeared duplicated, fragmented, or spread across neurons.
rows.note: This concerns feature interpretability and distribution across neurons, not polysemantic responses to unrelated inputs.
rows.check: Bottom-ranked MSAE latents are selected by the study's own minority score. This is a selection-based qualitative observation about SAE features, not about network neurons.

rows.subject: FLUX.1-schnell
rows.operation_detail: Qualitatively inspected high-scoring features, top-activating images, and attribution maps.
rows.measure: Qualitative interpretability and spatial grounding of discovered features
rows.value: The authors report a higher fraction of high-scoring but weakly interpretable neurons than in U-Net-based models; several candidates had diffuse or non-localized heatmaps.
rows.note: The comparison is about interpretability of RAIGen-discovered features, not polysemanticity rates.
rows.check: Measures interpretability of the method's own discovered features in FLUX vs U-Net, not polysemanticity rates of model neurons.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
